bib.title: Parametric Models and Exponential Families (ch. 5 of Computer Age Statistical Inference)

question: Which classic low-dimensional parametric families matter in computer-age statistics, and what common structure (exponential families) connects them?
contributions: Review of univariate families (normal, Poisson, binomial, gamma, beta)
Multivariate normal, conditional and Bayes posterior formulas
Fisher information bound for multiparameter MLE and the nuisance-parameter tax
Exponential families: tilting, natural/expectation parameters, cumulant-generating normaliser, MLE

Only exponential families compress an iid sample of any size n into a fixed p-dimensional sufficient statistic ybar.

results.quote: Only exponential families enjoy this property.

results.claim: In the exponential family, the MLE of the expectation parameter beta=E[y] is y (ybar); the MLE of natural parameter alpha needs inverting psi-dot, usually numerically (closed form e.g. log y for Poisson).
results.setup: p-parameter exponential family; eq 5.56-5.61, note 10: MLE solves E_alpha{y}=y
results.quote: The maximum likelihood estimate for the expectation parameter

results.claim: MLE is approximately N_p(theta, I^-1); extra nuisance parameters never decrease its variance: (I^-1)_11 >= 1/I_11.
results.setup: Smoothly parametrized p-dim family, large iid sample; Fisher information I = cov of score; eq 5.27-5.31
results.quote: must always increase4 in the presence of nuisance parameters.

results.claim: Poisson counts conditioned on their sum are multinomial; multinomial with Poisson(n) total is Poisson.
results.quote: removes the correlations and is usually quite accurate

limits: Brief review; chapter says it may be reviewed lightly at first reading.
MLE normality (5.27) is a large-sample approximation, no finite-n accuracy given.
Normaliser psi-dot inverse usually not closed form; numerics needed (Lindsey's method deferred to Ch 10).
Many derivations deferred to endnotes or other chapters; GLMs in Ch 8.
practices: Treat nonparametric as multinomial on discrete categories (p.64), as used by the bootstrap in Ch 10.
Use the Poisson approximation to the multinomial to remove correlations when n is large (p.64).
Beware nuisance parameters: unbiased/ML estimation pays a variance tax; biased methods (empirical Bayes Ch 6, l1 regression Ch 16) can reverse it (p.61).
Work with specially designed exponential families (e.g. polynomial sufficient statistics) rather than being limited to tractable classics (p.68).
